'''Norman Woodason Johnson''' (November 12, 1930 – July 13, 2017) was an American [[mathematician]] at [[Wheaton College, Massachusetts|Wheaton College]], [[Norton, Massachusetts]].{{r|Weiss}}

== Early life and education ==
Norman Johnson was born on {{date2|November|12, |1930}} in [[Chicago]]. His father had a bookstore and published a local newspaper.{{r|Weiss}}

Johnson earned his undergraduate mathematics degree in 1953 at [[Carleton College]] in [[Northfield, Minnesota]]{{refn|{{Cite web |date=July 18, 2017 |title=Norman Johnson '53 |url=https://www.carleton.edu/alumni/farewells/news/norman-johnson-53/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220519234859/https://www.carleton.edu/alumni/farewells/news/norman-johnson-53/ |archive-date=May 19, 2022 |access-date=May 19, 2022 |website=[[Carleton College]] |language=en-US}}}} followed by a master's degree from the [[University of Pittsburgh]].{{r|Weiss}} After graduating in 1953, Johnson did [[alternative civilian service]] as a [[conscientious objector]].{{r|Weiss}} He earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] from the [[University of Toronto]] in 1966 with a dissertation title of ''The Theory of Uniform Polytopes and Honeycombs'' under the supervision of  [[H. S. M. Coxeter]].{{ran|T66}} From there, he accepted a position in the Mathematics Department of Wheaton College in Massachusetts and taught until his retirement in 1998.{{r|Weiss}}

==Career==
In 1966, Johnson published a paper titled ''Convex Polyhedra with Regular Faces''.{{ran|A66}} Inside, it contained the list of 92 convex polyhedra with regular faces,{{r|Weiss}} along with the coined prefixes on naming some solids; encompassing the family of [[Prism (geometry)|prisms]], [[antiprism]]s, and other [[uniform polyhedra]] brings up 112 solids in total.{{r|Berman}} [[Victor Zalgaller]] later proved in 1969 that Johnson's list of 92 solids was complete, and the set is now known as the [[Johnson solid]]s or Johnson&ndash;Zalgaller solid.{{r|Zalgaller|Berman|AHU}}

Johnson is also credited with naming all the [[uniform star polyhedra]] and their [[Duality (mathematics)|duals]], as published in [[Magnus Wenninger]]'s model building books: ''Polyhedron models'' (1971) and ''Dual models'' (1983).{{refn|{{Cite book |last=Wenninger |first=Magnus |title=Dual Models |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=1983 |isbn=978-0-521-54325-5 |page=xii |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511569371 |mr=730208 |author-link=Magnus Wenninger}}}}

== Death and final works==
He completed final edits for his book ''Geometries and Transformations''{{ran|B18}} just before his death on {{date2|July|13, |2017}}, and nearly completed his manuscript on [[uniform polytope]]s.{{r|Weiss}}
